title: Anything You Want
subtitle: 40 Lessons for a New Kind of Entrepreneur
author: Derek Sivers
why_it_matters: A short, stubborn correction to the idea that a company has to get big to count. Sivers built CD Baby into a business worth tens of millions without taking a cent of outside money, then wrote the anti-playbook: revenue over funding, one delighted customer over a market study.

crux.headline: Design the small world you actually want to live in
crux.body: Most startup advice assumes you want scale, investors and an exit. Start somewhere else. Decide what kind of days you want, then build a business shaped to produce them. Fund it with customers instead of investors, so nobody else's timeline overrides yours. Stay small enough to still talk to the people who pay you. A company is an invented thing, and you are allowed to invent a different one.

sparks.hook: A company is an invented thing. You are allowed to invent a different one.
sparks.insight: Nothing about a business is handed down. Opening hours, who you serve, how big you get, whether you take investment, what happens when someone calls — every one of those is a choice somebody made, and you can make it differently. Most founders inherit a default shape from the people around them and then spend a decade unhappy inside it. Decide first what an ordinary Tuesday should feel like. Then work backwards to the business that produces that Tuesday, even if it looks nothing like the ones being written about.
sparks.why: Business form follows no natural law. The dominant model is dominant because it suits investors who need outsized returns, not because it is the only structure that survives contact with customers.
sparks.apply: Write a page describing your ideal working week in detail, then list every part of your current plan that quietly contradicts it.

sparks.hook: If nobody has paid you, you do not have a business yet.
sparks.insight: Enthusiasm is free, so people give it away. Friends say they love the idea, surveys say people would definitely buy, and none of that survives contact with a card reader. The only real signal is money leaving somebody else's account for the thing you made. That makes the fastest test of an idea also the cheapest: put a price on it and try to collect. If you cannot collect, you have learned something enormous in a week instead of after two funded years.
sparks.why: Stated intent and paid behaviour diverge badly, because saying yes to a survey costs nothing. Charging converts a vague opinion into a decision with a cost attached, and only that kind predicts anything.
sparks.apply: Take your current idea and try to sell one unit this week, before it is finished. Charge real money, even a small amount, and see who actually pays.

sparks.hook: If your answer is not an obvious yes, treat it as a no.
sparks.insight: Founders drown in decent opportunities. A partnership that might work, a client who is almost right, a feature one person asked for. Each is defensible on its own and together they eat the year. The filter is brutally simple: if a chance does not make you genuinely eager, refuse it. Saying no to the merely good is what leaves room for the rare thing worth everything you have. The cost of a mild yes is invisible, which is exactly why it keeps getting paid.
sparks.why: Your time is the fixed input. Mediocre commitments do not fail loudly, they just occupy the slot the exceptional thing needed, and you never get to see the trade you made.
sparks.apply: List every commitment currently on your plate. Mark each as genuinely exciting or merely fine, and start exiting one merely-fine item this month.

sparks.hook: You need no funding, no plan and no permission to begin this week.
sparks.insight: The gap between wanting to start and starting is usually filled with preparation nobody asked for: a plan, a brand, an entity, a round. Sivers began by selling one album from a page he coded himself, then added the next thing only when a musician asked for it. Starting tiny is not humility, it is speed of learning. You find out what people actually want while your costs are still near zero and there is nobody who can stop you changing direction.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: he could already code, and in the late nineties there was no other way for an independent musician to sell online. Scrappy starts still work, but a market opening that wide is rare and should not be assumed.
sparks.apply: Strip your idea to the smallest version you could deliver by hand to one person, and deliver it to that person before you register a company.

carousel.title: Sell before you build
carousel.body: Offer the thing to one real person and take their money first. What they ask for next is a better specification than anything you would have written alone in a room.

carousel.title: Keep costs near zero
carousel.body: Low overheads buy you the right to be wrong. No office, no hires and no debt means a bad month is a lesson rather than a crisis you must fundraise your way out of.

carousel.title: Add only what is asked for
carousel.body: Build the next feature when a paying customer requests it, not when you imagine somebody might. Requests arrive with evidence attached; imagination does not.

carousel.title: Delay the machinery
carousel.body: Entities, brand systems and funding rounds feel like progress and produce none. Set them up when revenue makes them necessary, not before.

sparks.hook: Your paying customers will write the roadmap if you let them.
sparks.insight: CD Baby's features arrived as a queue of small requests from musicians who were already paying. Someone needed a barcode, someone needed a sales report, so those got built next. This is unglamorous and it beats planning, because a request from a paying customer carries proof that at least one person wants it, and usually means dozens more do. The discipline is to ship the small thing quickly rather than bundling requests into a grand release that lands a year late.
sparks.why: A feature request from a paying user is a demand signal with money behind it. A feature from a roadmap workshop is a guess with a deadline behind it, and the deadline is the only part that is real.
sparks.apply: Start a running list of every unprompted customer request. Ship the smallest one this week and tell the person who asked that it is live.

sparks.hook: The dullest message you send is the cheapest place to be memorable.
sparks.insight: Every business has moments everybody treats as plumbing: the order confirmation, the invoice, the hold music, the packaging. Because they are ignored by default, a small amount of personality in one of them stands out enormously. Sivers rewrote his shipping confirmation as a piece of comic theatre and customers forwarded it to friends for years, which cost nothing and did more than advertising would have. Delight is cheapest exactly where nobody else bothers to look.
sparks.why: Attention is relative. A modest effort placed where the standard is zero reads as remarkable, while the same effort inside an already-crowded channel disappears without trace.
sparks.apply: Pick one routine message your business sends automatically and rewrite it as though a human wrote it for a person they liked.

sparks.hook: Being small can be the destination, not a stage you pass through.
sparks.insight: Growth is treated as automatic: get bigger until something stops you. But bigger buys you management, meetings, financing and a great many people whose problems are now yours. If the business already pays for the life you want, the question of what further growth is actually for deserves a real answer. Some of the best businesses ever run deliberately capped their size so the founder could keep doing the work instead of supervising it. Choosing not to expand is a strategy, not a failure of nerve.
sparks.why: Scale changes what your job is. Past a certain headcount you stop making the thing and start operating a system for making it, which many founders discover only once it is expensive to reverse.
sparks.apply: Calculate the annual revenue that would fund the life you want. Write it down, and treat everything above that line as optional rather than obligatory.

sparks.hook: Handing over the work is fine. Handing over your attention is not.
sparks.insight: Founders who hate managing often solve it by disappearing: appoint people, stop attending, hope. Sivers did a version of this and later found decisions being made in his own company that he would never have made himself. The alternative is not micromanagement. It is being transparent about how you decide. Write your reasoning down so other people can apply it without you in the room, then stay close enough to the work to notice when reality has drifted from the rules you wrote.
sparks.why: Delegation transfers a task; it does not transfer judgement. Judgement only transfers when the criteria behind your decisions are written somewhere other people can actually read them.
sparks.apply: Next time you settle a recurring decision, write the rule you used in one short paragraph and put it where your team can find it.

carousel.title: Decide out loud
carousel.body: When you make a judgement call, say why in front of people. The reasoning is the reusable part; the decision itself only solves today's version of the problem.

carousel.title: Write the rule down
carousel.body: Turn repeated reasoning into a short written policy anyone can apply. A team holding your criteria makes your decisions without having to wait for you.

carousel.title: Let them use it
carousel.body: Ask people to decide using the rule and tell you afterwards. Correcting a rule is cheap; approving every case one at a time is a full-time job you will resent.

carousel.title: Stay in the room
carousel.body: Keep standing contact with the work itself, not just the reports about it. Distance is how founders end up surprised by their own company.

sparks.hook: An idea is a multiplier on execution, and most multipliers are small.
sparks.insight: People guard ideas as though the idea were the asset. Treat it instead as a number that gets multiplied by what you actually build. A brilliant idea with nothing built is still worth nothing, because anything times zero is zero. A modest idea executed well beats a spectacular one described well, every time. This is why secrecy is usually wasted energy: telling somebody your idea costs you close to nothing, while getting an honest reaction to it can change what you build.
sparks.why: The scarce input is finished work, not conception. Ideas are abundant and cheap to generate; the willingness to spend years making one of them real is not.
sparks.apply: Tell three people your idea in full this week and ask each what would stop them buying it, then build the smallest testable piece.

sparks.hook: Say clearly who you are not for, and the right people will find you.
sparks.insight: Trying to be acceptable to everyone produces a business nobody chooses on purpose. Naming your exclusions does the opposite: it tells a smaller group that this thing was made specifically for them. CD Baby existed for independent musicians shut out by the major labels, which was a narrow claim and exactly why those musicians felt it belonged to them. A sharp no to most of the market is what makes the yes worth having.
sparks.why: Positioning works by contrast. A business that fits everybody has no contrast to trade on, so nothing about it is distinct enough for a customer to describe to a friend.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence naming the customer your business is deliberately not for, and put it somewhere public on your website.

actions: Write a one-page description of the life you want this business to fund, then audit your current plan against it and cut the parts that only serve someone else's idea of success.
Charge money for the smallest usable version of your idea this month, even if you deliver it by hand, and treat the first payment as your only real validation.
Start a decisions file. Each time you settle a recurring question, write down the rule and the reasoning so somebody else can apply it without asking you.
Rewrite one routine customer message so it sounds like a person wrote it, then watch whether anyone mentions it unprompted.
not_for_you_if: You are raising venture money and need tactics for scale. This is a short personal account of doing the opposite, and it does not pretend to be a general system.

verification.notes: Published 2011 by The Domino Project. All prose original; no wording reproduced from the book.

title: Blitzscaling
subtitle: The Lightning-Fast Path to Building Massively Valuable Companies
author: Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh
why_it_matters: It names and defends a strategy Silicon Valley had been running for a decade without a manual: choose speed over efficiency while a winner-take-most market is still open. Useful as much for showing you when not to do it.

crux.headline: Trade efficiency for speed when the prize is winner-take-most
crux.body: Blitzscaling is prioritising growth over sane management while a market is still up for grabs. You accept known waste, unfinished products and half-run departments to reach scale before a rival does. It is a bet, not a virtue, and it only pays where network effects, huge market size and strong margins let a leader lock in the position. Everywhere else it is a costly way to buy customers who leave.

sparks.hook: Growing faster than you can manage is sometimes the correct decision.
sparks.insight: Blitzscaling means choosing to grow faster than you can comfortably run the company, deliberately, while the market is still open. You will hire people you would not hire in calmer times, ship things that are unfinished, and let whole functions operate badly. That is the trade: known waste in exchange for reaching scale before anybody else can. Efficiency is what you buy later with the position you won. The mistake is not the chaos, it is running the play without admitting you are placing a bet.
sparks.why: Where one winner takes most of the value, being second with a cleaner operation is worth far less than being first with a messy one. Outside those markets the same behaviour is just an expensive way to fail.
sparks.apply: Before spending on speed, write down the specific mechanism that would let a leader lock in this market. If you cannot name one, optimise for margin instead.

sparks.hook: Most companies should never blitzscale, and yours is probably one.
sparks.insight: The strategy only pays when the market has winner-take-most dynamics: real network effects, a very large addressable market, or distribution that compounds. Without those, growing faster than your economics simply converts investor money into customers who churn. The advice also has an era attached. It was written when capital was abundant and cheap, and the same playbook wrecked companies once funding tightened. Read it as a conditional strategy with a short list of preconditions, not as a description of how ambitious companies behave.
sparks.why: The famous examples are survivors selected after the fact. For every company that outran its own chaos, many did the identical things and ran out of money before scale ever arrived.
sparks.apply: Score your market honestly on network effects, size, gross margin and distribution. Two weak scores out of the four means the answer is no.

sparks.hook: Four properties decide whether fast growth can actually stick.
sparks.insight: Some businesses can absorb explosive growth and some cannot, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of effort. Market size caps how far you can run. Distribution decides how cheaply you reach the next customer. Gross margin decides how much of each sale is left over to fund the next one. Network effects decide whether early scale makes you harder to beat or merely bigger. Check all four before you spend, because a weakness in any one turns aggressive growth into an expensive treadmill.
sparks.why: These are the properties that make growth self-reinforcing rather than self-funded. A business missing them can still be excellent; it just has to be built patiently instead of quickly.
sparks.apply: Rate your business from one to five on each of the four factors, then show the ratings to somebody who has no reason to flatter you.

carousel.title: Size the real market
carousel.body: Count the customers who could plausibly buy, not the industry the analysts describe. A market that is too small caps your outcome however well you execute.

carousel.title: Find compounding distribution
carousel.body: Look for a channel whose cost per customer falls as you grow: referrals, a platform, an existing user base. Paid channels that stay expensive cannot carry this strategy.

carousel.title: Protect gross margin
carousel.body: High margin means each sale funds the next one. Thin margins mean growth burns cash faster the better it goes, which is the worst kind of success.

carousel.title: Test for network effects
carousel.body: Ask whether each new user makes the product measurably better for the existing ones. If not, scale gives you size with no defence attached.

sparks.hook: Two things stop growth: nobody wants it, or you cannot serve them.
sparks.insight: Growth stalls for boring reasons. Either people do not want the thing enough to stay, or the company physically cannot serve more of them without falling over. The first is fatal and cannot be spent past, since pouring money on weak product fit buys you a bigger leak. The second is solvable, but only with time, hiring and systems, which is why founders in a hypergrowth phase spend their nights on operations rather than strategy. Diagnose which one is biting before you pick a remedy.
sparks.why: Marketing amplifies whatever the product already does. If retention is weak, amplification raises your costs and your churn at the same time and hides the problem behind a rising top line.
sparks.apply: Look at retention by signup cohort before you increase spend. If cohorts decay to zero, fix the product; if they flatten and hold, fix the operations.

sparks.hook: Your job changes completely each time headcount multiplies by ten.
sparks.insight: A company at five people, fifty, five hundred and five thousand is four different organisms wearing the same name. What works at each size actively breaks the next one. At the smallest scale everyone does everything and information travels because you can hear each other. Later you need specialists, written process, managers of managers, and a way to communicate that does not depend on your voice reaching the room. Founders usually fail not by doing the wrong thing but by continuing to do the thing that worked one stage ago.
sparks.why: Coordination cost grows faster than headcount does. The structures that feel like bureaucracy at ten people are the same ones that stop five hundred people working at cross purposes.
sparks.apply: Write down the three habits that make your team effective today, then ask which of them becomes impossible at four times your current size.

carousel.title: Everyone does everything
carousel.body: At a handful of people, generalists win and process is pure overhead. Communication happens because you can overhear it. Optimise for range and speed, not job titles.

carousel.title: Hire the first specialists
carousel.body: In the tens, gaps open that a generalist cannot fill. Bring in people genuinely better than you at one thing, and let them own it rather than reviewing their every move.

carousel.title: Manage the managers
carousel.body: In the hundreds you stop directing work and start choosing the people who direct work. Your leverage becomes hiring, standards, and deciding what the company will not do.

carousel.title: Broadcast, do not chat
carousel.body: Past a certain size you cannot repeat context in conversation. Write things down, say them repeatedly in public, and accept that under-communicating is now the default failure.

sparks.hook: You cannot put out every fire. Choose the one that kills you.
sparks.insight: A fast-growing company is on fire in several places at once: support is drowning, the infrastructure is fragile, finance is improvised, half the team is unmanaged. Trying to fix everything guarantees everything gets fixed badly. Rank the fires by what actually ends the company this quarter, put your attention there, and consciously let the others burn. Letting something burn is a decision you make and announce, not neglect you apologise for eighteen months later.
sparks.why: Attention is the binding constraint in a scaling company, not money. Spreading it evenly across problems of wildly different severity is how founders end up with a dozen half-solved crises.
sparks.apply: List every problem you know about and mark only the ones that could end the company within ninety days. Work those, and tell your team the rest are deferred.

sparks.hook: Hire the person who fits the next year, not the next decade.
sparks.insight: Founders stall for months hunting an executive who could run the function at a size the company may never reach. In a fast-moving business the role will be unrecognisable in eighteen months anyway, so the candidate who is excellent for the stage you are actually in beats the impressive one waiting for you to catch up. This does mean people will outgrow their jobs, and the honest version involves saying so at offer stage rather than pretending every hire is permanent.
sparks.why: Stage fit predicts performance better than pedigree, because the required skills genuinely differ by stage. The real cost is turnover among your leaders, which is uncomfortable and often handled badly.
sparks.apply: Write the job description for the next twelve months only, hire against that, and say plainly in the offer conversation that the role will change.

sparks.hook: Do the unscalable thing now and plan to throw it away.
sparks.insight: Manual work that could never survive at scale is often the fastest route to scale. Onboard the first customers yourself, deliver the service by hand, personally recruit the first hundred users. It teaches you precisely what the product must eventually automate, and it produces customers who stay because a person paid attention to them. The discipline is treating it as temporary scaffolding with a planned demolition date, instead of accidentally building your company around permanent heroics.
sparks.why: Manual delivery gives you high-resolution information about what customers actually need, which is exactly what you lack early on. It only fails when nobody ever decides to replace it.
sparks.apply: Pick one part of your product you plan to automate and do it by hand for ten customers first, writing down every exception you hit.

sparks.hook: The crew that wins the raid cannot be trusted to run the fleet.
sparks.insight: Early teams win by being fast, informal and slightly lawless. Later the same company needs predictability, coordination and people who will follow a plan they did not invent. Both cultures are correct for their moment, which is what makes the transition so painful: the people who got you here are being asked to behave in the exact way that would once have killed the company. Handle it explicitly. Name the change, explain why, and find new roles for those who cannot make the switch.
sparks.why: Neither mode is superior. What changes is the cost of error: at five people an unreviewed decision is cheap, at five hundred it silently commits hundreds of hours of other people's work.
sparks.apply: Name one process you have resisted adding because it feels corporate, then add the lightest possible version of it this quarter.

sparks.hook: Speed transfers risk onto people who never agreed to the bet.
sparks.insight: Growing faster than you can govern means shipping decisions before you understand them. Safety work gets postponed, moderation gets outsourced, and the people carrying the cost are usually users, contractors and the cities the company moves through, rather than the founders or the investors. Hoffman is unusually direct about this and still concludes the strategy is worth running, which is the part worth arguing with. If you choose speed, know whose downside you are spending.
sparks.why: The last decade supplied the evidence. Platforms scaled well past their ability to police what they had built, and the correction arrived as regulation, litigation and permanently lost trust.
sparks.apply: List three harms your product could cause at a hundred times its current size, and decide now which one you will resource before it happens.

actions: Score your market on network effects, addressable size, gross margin and distribution cost, and only consider a growth-at-all-costs plan if all four are strong.
Build a cohort retention chart before you raise your marketing budget, and treat decaying cohorts as a signal to stop spending rather than to spend harder.
Write down the three biggest fires in your company, pick the single one that could kill you this quarter, and tell your team the others are deliberately deferred.
Draft the twelve-month version of your next senior job description, and rehearse the honest conversation about how the role will change as you grow.
not_for_you_if: You run a services, retail or hardware business with normal margins. Almost none of this applies, and following it would mean spending money you can never earn back.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Currency. Written during an era of unusually cheap capital; several of its case companies later contracted sharply. Prose here is original.

title: The Startup Owner's Manual
subtitle: The Step-by-Step Guide for Building a Great Company
author: Steve Blank and Bob Dorf
why_it_matters: The full checklist version of customer development, the method that gave the lean startup movement its engine. Nearly every accelerator curriculum in the world is a compressed version of what is set out here.

crux.headline: A startup is a search party, not a small company
crux.body: An established company executes a business model it already understands. A startup has only a stack of guesses about who the customer is, what hurts, and what they will pay. Confusing the two makes you build the wrong thing efficiently. Organise to search instead: numbered assumptions, cheap tests run by the founders themselves, and a rule that failing a test sends you backwards rather than forwards.

sparks.hook: A startup is not a small company. It is a search party.
sparks.insight: A company executes a business model it already knows. A startup does not have one yet — it has a set of guesses about who the customer is, what problem they have, and what they will pay. Confusing the two is the most expensive mistake in early business. If you organise like a company, with a sales target, a launch date and a functional org chart, you will spend the money building the wrong thing very efficiently. Organise to search instead: cheap experiments, fast rewrites, no permanent structures.
sparks.why: The failure mode is structural rather than personal. Execution machinery makes commitments hard to reverse, and a search phase needs everything to stay reversible until the model is proven.
sparks.apply: Write your business model as a list of numbered guesses. Mark the one that kills everything if it is wrong, and go and test that one first.

sparks.hook: There are no facts inside your building. Go outside and get some.
sparks.insight: Everything inside the office is opinion dressed as analysis: your roadmap, your persona document, your pricing, your competitive matrix. The facts live with the people who might pay you, and the only way to get them is to sit in front of those people repeatedly and ask. Founders have to do this themselves rather than hiring a research agency, because the point is not the report. The point is that the person deciding what to build has heard a customer be unimpressed, in their own voice.
sparks.why: Second-hand research strips out the tone, the hesitation and the ugly workaround the customer has already built, which is usually where the actual product is hiding.
sparks.apply: Book five conversations this week with people who fit your target customer, and ask about their current workaround before you describe your product at all.

sparks.hook: Four steps stand between a guess and a company that can scale.
sparks.insight: Customer development runs in a fixed order, and skipping ahead is why startups explode. First you discover whether the problem and the customer are real. Then you validate that you can sell the solution repeatedly, yourself, at a price that works. Only then do you spend on creating demand, and only after that do you convert the search team into a functioning organisation. Each step has an exit test, and failing it sends you backwards rather than forwards. That backwards move is what a pivot actually is.
sparks.why: The order encodes cost. Every step forward multiplies your burn rate, so proving the cheap things first is what keeps a wrong answer survivable rather than terminal.
sparks.apply: Identify which of the four steps you are honestly in right now, then stop any spending that properly belongs to a later step.

carousel.title: Discover the problem
carousel.body: Turn your assumptions into testable statements and take them to real customers. You are looking for a problem people already spend time or money trying to solve badly.

carousel.title: Validate the sale
carousel.body: Sell to strangers with the founders doing the selling. If you cannot close repeatedly without heroics, you have not found a business model yet, only interest.

carousel.title: Create demand
carousel.body: Now spend on marketing to pull buyers into the funnel. How much you spend and how you spend it depends entirely on which kind of market you are entering.

carousel.title: Build the company
carousel.body: Only once the model repeats do you replace the search team with departments, process and the ordinary machinery of execution.

sparks.hook: The kind of market you enter changes every number in your plan.
sparks.insight: Entering an existing market is a race on features against known rivals, and customers already understand what you sell. Creating a new market means nobody is searching for you, adoption takes years, and your early budget goes on education rather than competition. Resegmenting means carving a niche or a cheaper position inside somebody else's market. Cloning means bringing a proven model to a new country. These paths have completely different spending curves, and borrowing the wrong one's plan is a reliable way to die on schedule.
sparks.why: Market type determines when revenue can plausibly arrive. New-market companies that budget like existing-market companies run out of cash during the education phase, which was always the expected phase.
sparks.apply: Name your market type in one word, then rebuild your first three years of forecasts around its adoption curve rather than a competitor's.

sparks.hook: Your first customers should already be trying to fix this themselves.
sparks.insight: The best early buyers are not the ones who enjoy your demo. They are people who have the problem, know they have it, have gone looking for a solution, and have already improvised something ugly — a spreadsheet, a manual process, three tools taped together. That improvisation is the strongest evidence of demand you will ever get, and it also means they will tolerate your unfinished product, because their current alternative is worse. Selling to anyone earlier on that ladder means doing the customer's realising for them.
sparks.why: Awareness of a problem is a prerequisite for buying. A customer who has not yet built a workaround is telling you the pain has not reached the threshold where money moves.
sparks.apply: For each prospect, ask what they do about this problem today. Deprioritise anyone whose honest answer is that they do nothing at all.

sparks.hook: A pivot is a change to the model, not a change of mind.
sparks.insight: The word gets used for any wobble, which makes it useless. Use it precisely: a pivot is a substantive change to one component of the business model — the customer, the problem, the channel, the pricing, the value proposition — made because a test told you the current version is wrong. That definition has teeth. It means a pivot requires a failed test to justify it, it means you change one component and re-test rather than rebuilding everything, and it means constant pivoting is a sign you are not testing at all.
sparks.why: Naming the specific component stops you discarding the parts that were working. Most failed pivots throw away validated learning along with the broken assumption, and start again from zero.
sparks.apply: Before your next big change, write down which single component of the model is changing and what evidence forced it. If you cannot, it is not a pivot.

sparks.hook: Do not hire a salesperson until you have sold it yourself.
sparks.insight: Founders often treat selling as beneath them and hire a sales team to find out whether the product sells. It never works, because the first sales are not a sales job. They are research that happens to produce revenue. Until you know who buys, which objection kills the deal, what creates urgency and what price sticks, there is no roadmap for a salesperson to follow, so you are asking somebody to execute a process nobody has discovered. Sell it yourself until the sale is boringly repeatable.
sparks.why: An early sales hire fails for structural reasons and then looks like a bad hire. The company loses a year and frequently concludes, wrongly, that the market was the problem.
sparks.apply: Set an explicit threshold before your first sales hire, such as ten closed deals you personally ran using the same pitch and the same price.

sparks.hook: Build the smallest thing capable of proving you wrong.
sparks.insight: A minimum viable product is not a cheap version of the finished product. It is an instrument for answering one question you currently cannot answer, built to the lowest fidelity that still gives a trustworthy answer. Sometimes that means working software, and often it means a page, a document, a demo or a service you perform by hand. The test of a good one is not whether customers like it but whether their reaction changes what you do next. If every outcome leaves your plan unchanged, you built the wrong instrument.
sparks.why: Cost per experiment sets how many wrong guesses you can survive. Anything in the build that does not serve the current question is money you will not get back.
sparks.apply: Write the question your next build answers, plus the two possible results and the different action each would trigger, before anyone writes code.

carousel.title: State the question
carousel.body: Name the single uncertainty that matters most right now, phrased so that it can come back false. Vague questions produce builds that cannot fail and therefore cannot teach.

carousel.title: Pick the cheapest instrument
carousel.body: Choose the lowest-fidelity thing that would still convince you: a landing page, a manual service, a clickable mock. Fidelity costs money and rarely changes the answer.

carousel.title: Set the threshold first
carousel.body: Decide before the test what result counts as a pass. Deciding afterwards guarantees you will find some way to read the data as encouraging.

carousel.title: Run it on strangers
carousel.body: Test with people who have no relationship with you. Friends and advisers give you politeness, which is indistinguishable from demand right up until you invoice.

carousel.title: Act on the answer
carousel.body: Write down the decision the result forces and take it within the week. An experiment nobody acts on is an expensive kind of procrastination.

sparks.hook: Failing a checkpoint sends you backwards. That is the system working.
sparks.insight: Every stage of customer development has an exit condition, and if you do not meet it the instruction is to go back, not to press on with a smaller version of the same plan. That is uncomfortable, because backwards looks like failure to everybody watching, investors included. But the alternative is scaling a model you have not proven, which converts a recoverable setback into an unrecoverable one. Startups that die have usually passed a checkpoint they had actually failed.
sparks.why: The cost of continuing rises steeply at each step, so an unproven assumption carried forward gets more expensive the longer it goes unexamined, and harder to admit to.
sparks.apply: Define the pass condition for your current stage in one measurable sentence, and agree with your co-founders in advance what happens if you miss it.

sparks.hook: This is a manual, not a book. Use it like one.
sparks.insight: It runs to several hundred pages of checklists and is close to unreadable cover to cover, which is a format rather than a flaw. Used properly you open it at the stage you are in, follow the specific list for that stage, and close it again. That makes it far more useful as a shared reference for a founding team than as something one person reads alone. The checklist form also imposes a real discipline: it is much harder to pretend you completed a step when the step has a list attached.
sparks.why: Checklists work by removing reliance on memory and optimism, the same reason they hold up in aviation and surgery. Their weakness is that they invite box-ticking in place of judgement.
sparks.apply: Print the checklist for the single stage you are actually in, put it on the wall, and review it with your co-founder every Friday.

actions: Write your business model out as numbered assumptions, rank them by how fatal each would be if wrong, and design a cheap test for the top three this month.
Do ten customer conversations yourself, with no slides, asking only about how they handle the problem today and what that workaround costs them.
Name your market type in writing and rebuild your revenue forecast around the adoption curve that type implies, not the one your pitch deck wants.
Agree a written pass condition for your current stage with your co-founders, including what you will do if the condition is not met.
not_for_you_if: You want an evening read or a narrative. This is a dense reference volume of checklists, and reading it straight through will exhaust you well before it helps you.

verification.notes: Published 2012 by K&S Ranch. Expands the customer development method Blank first set out in 2005. Prose here is original.

title: Hooked
subtitle: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
author: Nir Eyal
why_it_matters: It gave product teams a shared vocabulary for how software becomes automatic, and that vocabulary went on to shape a decade of consumer apps. Worth reading as a description of what is being done to your attention, not only as a toolkit.

crux.headline: Habits are built by a loop, not by persuasion
crux.body: A product becomes automatic through a cycle that runs repeatedly: something prompts you, you take an easy action, you get a reward that varies, and then you put something of your own in. Each pass makes the next more likely, until an internal feeling replaces the external prompt. Design each of the four stages deliberately, and ask honestly whether the habit you are building is one the user would thank you for.

sparks.hook: Habit-forming products do not persuade you. They train you.
sparks.insight: A product becomes a habit when using it stops being a decision. That happens through a loop that runs over and over: something prompts you, you take a small action, you get a reward that varies, and then you put something of your own into the product. Each pass makes the next one more likely, until an internal feeling — boredom, anxiety, loneliness — is enough to trigger the behaviour with no nudge from outside. Once that link forms, the product no longer needs advertising to bring you back.
sparks.why: The mechanism draws on well-established learning research and on the Fogg behaviour model. What is far less established is the case selection, which comes from products that had already succeeded.
sparks.apply: Map one of your own daily app habits through the four stages, and name the internal feeling that triggers it before the phone ever does.

sparks.hook: Trigger, action, reward, investment. Then the whole thing runs again.
sparks.insight: The loop has four parts and each does a different job. Triggers start the behaviour, first from outside and eventually from inside your own head. The action is the simplest thing you can do in anticipation of a reward, so it has to be trivially easy. The reward must vary, because a payoff you can predict stops holding attention. The investment is what you put in — data, content, followers, effort — which both improves the product for you and gives you a reason to return to what you built.
sparks.why: The parts are dependent on one another. A product with a great reward but a hard action fails, and one with an easy action and a fixed reward gets boring inside a fortnight.
sparks.apply: Take one feature you are building and write out its four stages on a single page. Fix whichever stage you find you cannot fill in.

carousel.title: Start with the trigger
carousel.body: External prompts get people in the door: a notification, a link, a recommendation. The aim is to attach the behaviour to an internal feeling so the prompt becomes unnecessary.

carousel.title: Make the action trivial
carousel.body: Behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt line up. Ability is the cheapest to change, so cut steps until the action takes one tap and no thought.

carousel.title: Vary the reward
carousel.body: Unpredictable payoffs hold attention far better than fixed ones. Rewards arrive as social approval, as the hunt for something good, or as a felt sense of progress.

carousel.title: Ask for an investment
carousel.body: Get people to add something: a profile, a playlist, a review, a connection. Stored value makes the product better next time and makes leaving feel like a loss.

sparks.hook: Easy beats motivating. Remove a step before you add a reason.
sparks.insight: When somebody does not do the thing you want, the instinct is to persuade harder. Usually the cheaper fix is to make the action simpler. Behaviour needs three things at once: enough motivation, enough ability, and a prompt. Motivation is expensive and unstable, prompts are easy but irritating, and ability is the one you can actually engineer. Cutting a form field, removing a login step, defaulting a choice — each of those does more for adoption than any amount of copy about why the product is good.
sparks.why: This comes from the Fogg behaviour model, a design heuristic rather than a strong empirical law. It holds up in practice because friction reliably suppresses low-motivation behaviour.
sparks.apply: Count the taps between opening your product and the first moment of real value, then delete one of those steps this week.

sparks.hook: A reward that always arrives eventually stops being a reward.
sparks.insight: Predictability kills interest. A feed that always shows the same thing, a game you always win, a notification that always says the same words — each becomes background noise fast. Variation keeps the searching behaviour alive, because the outcome is worth checking. That is why feeds are endless, why loot boxes exist and why pulling to refresh feels like something. It is also the part of the model carrying the most ethical weight, since the same mechanism sits underneath a slot machine.
sparks.why: Variable reinforcement is among the most replicated findings in learning research. Its sheer strength is exactly what makes it easy to use against the person on the other end.
sparks.apply: Find one place your product is predictable and add genuine variety of value there, not a random number. Novelty with no substance stops working quickly.

sparks.hook: The work people put in is what stops them leaving later.
sparks.insight: Effort creates attachment. A playlist you curated, a profile you filled in, a network you built, a skill you learned inside an interface — all of it is value stored in the product that you cannot take with you. This is why the fourth stage of the loop is asked for after the reward rather than before: people invest far more readily once they have already received something. Stored value also loads the next trigger, because your own contributions give the product something new to tell you about.
sparks.why: People overvalue what they had a hand in making, an effect robust enough to appear in laboratory studies of self-assembled furniture and folded paper. Switching cost then does the rest of the work.
sparks.apply: Identify what your users accumulate inside your product over time. If the honest answer is nothing, design one thing genuinely worth accumulating.

sparks.hook: Ask which feeling your product gets used to relieve.
sparks.insight: External triggers get replaced by internal ones, and internal triggers are nearly always uncomfortable emotions: boredom, loneliness, uncertainty, the fear of missing something. A habit forms when your product becomes the fastest available relief for one specific feeling. That tells you where to look when designing — not at features, but at the moment of discomfort you can reliably resolve. It also explains why competing on features rarely dislodges an incumbent habit. The incumbent owns the feeling.
sparks.why: Emotion-linked cues are learned quickly and fire without deliberation, which is what makes them so much more durable than a reminder you have to consciously notice.
sparks.apply: Write down the exact feeling a user has in the ten seconds before they open your product, and design the first screen to resolve that feeling.

sparks.hook: If nobody would miss it after a week, it is not a habit.
sparks.insight: Habit-forming is a frequency question before it is a design question. A behaviour that recurs often enough, and delivers enough perceived value each time, can become automatic. A behaviour that happens twice a year cannot, however good the interface is. Before investing in engagement mechanics, check whether the underlying need actually shows up frequently. Insurance, house moves and tax filing are not habit businesses, and trying to force them into that shape wastes money a better first-use experience would have earned.
sparks.why: Automaticity requires repetition against a stable cue. Without natural frequency there is nothing to repeat, so the product manufactures occasions instead, and users experience that as nagging.
sparks.apply: Estimate how often a typical user genuinely needs what you do. If the answer is monthly or rarer, invest in making the single use excellent.

sparks.hook: Ask two questions before you make anything deliberately sticky.
sparks.insight: The same techniques that build a habit people are grateful for can build one they resent. Eyal offers a blunt test with two axes: does this materially improve the user's life, and would you use it yourself? Two yeses put you on solid ground. If you would use it but it does not really help, you are in entertainment, which is honest enough. If it helps but you would not touch it, be careful. If neither holds, you are extracting value from people rather than making any, whatever the marketing says.
sparks.why: The test is a moral heuristic, not a shield. It is easy to convince yourself a product helps when your revenue depends on believing that, so it works best applied by somebody outside the company.
sparks.apply: Run both questions past a person who is not paid by your company, and write down every place their answer differs from yours.

carousel.title: Would you use it
carousel.body: Answer honestly for yourself, not for a persona. Builders who would not touch their own product are usually relying on the user knowing less than they do.

carousel.title: Does it improve a life
carousel.body: Not entertain, not occupy: improve. Ask what the user would say a year later about the hours they spent, and whether they would call it time well spent.

carousel.title: Name who pays the cost
carousel.body: If attention is the product, somebody is paying in hours. Write down whose hours and how many, then decide whether the trade survives being explained to them.

carousel.title: Build the exit
carousel.body: Give people real controls: honest defaults, easy off switches, no dark patterns on cancellation. A habit that survives an easy exit is a habit you actually earned.

sparks.hook: Measure whether the habit exists instead of assuming it does.
sparks.insight: You can test for habit formation rather than hoping for it. Find the users who stuck around, look at what they did in their first days that the leavers did not, then deliberately push new users through that same sequence. This turns an abstract goal into a specific onboarding change. It also protects you from a common illusion: a growing user count can hide the fact that almost nobody returns, because fresh signups keep replacing the people quietly leaving out the back.
sparks.why: Cohort behaviour separates acquisition from retention. Aggregate numbers blur the two together and can climb for months while the underlying product gets steadily worse.
sparks.apply: Compare the first-week behaviour of users still active after two months against those who left, then pick one difference to design around.

sparks.hook: The person who wrote this manual later wrote the antidote.
sparks.insight: This is a growth manual, and the decade after it appeared showed exactly what growth teams do with one. Engagement techniques scaled into infinite feeds, streak mechanics aimed at teenagers, and notification systems tuned to interrupt. Eyal went on to write about resisting precisely these designs, which is a useful admission. Read the model as a description of how attention gets captured and you gain a defence as well as a weapon. Read it only as a toolkit and you will build something you would not want your own family using.
sparks.why: The techniques are neutral only in the limited sense that any powerful method is. What decides the outcome is whose interest the designer optimises for, and the incentives usually point one way.
sparks.apply: Audit your product for one mechanic you would struggle to justify to a regulator, and remove it before anybody asks you to.

actions: Write out the four stages of the loop for your product's core behaviour, and rebuild whichever stage you cannot describe in a single concrete sentence.
Time the path from opening your product to the first moment of value, then remove one step from it and measure the effect on week-one retention.
Ask somebody outside your company whether the product genuinely improves a user's life, and write down honestly where their answer differs from yours.
Compare the first-week behaviour of long-term users against those who churned, and redesign onboarding around the single biggest difference.
not_for_you_if: You want rigorous behavioural science with the evidence weighed. This is a practitioner framework built from successful products, and the causal claims are looser than they sound.

verification.notes: Published 2014, co-written with Ryan Hoover, who is generally credited as collaborator rather than co-author. Eyal's later work argues the other side. Prose original.

title: Lost and Founder
subtitle: A Painfully Honest Field Guide to the Startup World
author: Rand Fishkin
why_it_matters: A founder who did not win writing candidly about why, while most startup books are written by the survivors. Fishkin publishes the numbers, the debt, the depression and the board dynamics that the usual account leaves out.

crux.headline: The startup story you have been sold is heavily edited
crux.body: Almost everything published about building companies comes from people it worked out for, which makes the advice look far more reliable than it is. Fishkin describes the version underneath: raising money narrows what counts as success, growth targets set by a board override your own judgement, and the founder's health is treated as an infinite resource. Knowing that changes which choices you make while they are still cheap to reverse.

sparks.hook: Startup advice comes almost entirely from people it worked out for.
sparks.insight: The books, the conference talks and the podcasts share one hidden property: they were made by winners. Companies that did the same things and failed do not get invited to speak, so their evidence never enters the record. The result is advice that sounds like a method and is closer to a description of what lucky people happened to do. Fishkin's account is unusual because he tells it from inside a company that survived without ever reaching the outcome its funding assumed, and describes what that felt like.
sparks.why: Selecting cases on the outcome is one of the oldest errors in reasoning about causes. Without the failures you cannot tell which behaviours mattered and which merely accompanied a good result.
sparks.apply: For every piece of founder advice you adopt, ask what a company that followed it and failed would look like, and whether you would ever have heard of them.

sparks.hook: Raising money quietly deletes most of your acceptable outcomes.
sparks.insight: Before you take venture capital, a profitable company with steady growth is a great result. Afterwards it is a disappointment, because the fund's economics only work if a small number of investments return enormous multiples. Nobody has to be dishonest for this to bite. The maths of the fund simply reprices every option you have, and choices that would build a durable business start looking like a lack of ambition to the people around your board table. Decide whether you want that repricing before you sign, not afterwards.
sparks.why: A venture fund needs a handful of outsized exits to return the whole portfolio, so the pressure toward risky, growth-maximising strategy is structural rather than a matter of any individual investor's temperament.
sparks.apply: Write down what outcome would make you personally happy in seven years, then ask whether a fund's return model can tolerate that outcome.

sparks.hook: A sale can be a headline win and leave founders with nothing.
sparks.insight: Investor shares usually come with liquidation preferences, meaning that money goes back to them first when a company is sold. Stack a few rounds of that and a sale price that sounds impressive can be entirely consumed before ordinary shares see anything. Founders and employees hold those ordinary shares. Most people learn this after the wire arrives. The terms of a round matter at least as much as the valuation, and the valuation is the only number anybody talks about at the time.
sparks.why: Preferences, participation rights and multiples are contract terms, not market forces. They are negotiable at signing and effectively fixed forever afterwards, which makes early inattention permanent.
sparks.apply: Ask a lawyer to model your last term sheet at three sale prices, including a mediocre one, and see what your own shares receive in each.

carousel.title: Read the preference stack
carousel.body: List each round, the money raised and whatever preference attaches to it. That total gets paid before common shareholders receive anything at all in a sale.

carousel.title: Model a mediocre exit
carousel.body: Everyone models the great outcome. Run the numbers on a decent-but-unspectacular sale, which is statistically the most likely liquidity event you will ever face.

carousel.title: Check participation terms
carousel.body: Some preferences pay out and then share in the remainder too. That single clause can cost employees more than the headline valuation ever gave them.

carousel.title: Tell your team the truth
carousel.body: Explain what their options are really worth under realistic outcomes. People make life decisions on these numbers and deserve the arithmetic, not the pitch.

sparks.hook: Build the audience before you build the thing you will sell.
sparks.insight: Moz was a consultancy with an unusually generous blog long before it was a software company, and the audience that blog attracted became the distribution the software launched into. That ordering is the whole advantage. Most products fail not because they are bad but because nobody was waiting for them. An audience earned by being useful for years in public is slow to build and almost impossible for a competitor to buy, and it converts far better than any paid channel.
sparks.why: Distribution is usually scarcer than product capability. Building an audience first means the launch has an audience by construction, rather than depending on a channel you have never tested.
sparks.apply: Publish something genuinely useful to your target customer every week for three months before your product is ready, and track who subscribes.

carousel.title: Choose one audience
carousel.body: Name a single group narrowly enough that you could list where they gather. An audience defined as everybody produces content nobody feels was written for them.

carousel.title: Give away your best work
carousel.body: Publish the thing you would normally charge for. Holding back the useful parts is what makes most company content worthless and unshared.

carousel.title: Keep an unglamorous schedule
carousel.body: Publish on a fixed rhythm for long enough to feel pointless. Audience growth is slow and compounding, and most people stop during the flat part.

carousel.title: Own the connection
carousel.body: Move readers onto a list or channel you control. An audience that lives entirely on somebody else's platform can be taken away without notice.

carousel.title: Launch into the room
carousel.body: When the product is ready, you are introducing it to people who already trust you, rather than paying strangers to consider it for eight seconds.

sparks.hook: Publishing your own numbers is a strategy, not a confession.
sparks.insight: Moz put out revenue, salary bands, board material and accounts of its own failures, at a time when almost nobody did. It cost something: competitors learned things, and bad quarters were public. It also bought a level of trust that marketing cannot purchase, made recruiting easier and forced internal honesty, because a number you must publish is a number you cannot quietly reframe. Transparency works as a strategy specifically when your market rewards being believed.
sparks.why: Disclosure is credible precisely because it is costly. Anyone can claim to be trustworthy; publishing figures that could embarrass you is a signal that a dishonest company cannot cheaply copy.
sparks.apply: Pick one metric you have been vague about with your team or customers and publish it, along with what you plan to do about it.

sparks.hook: A minimum viable product only works if nobody is watching yet.
sparks.insight: Shipping something rough and learning from the reaction is sound advice when you are unknown, because a bad first version reaches ten people who will try again later. Once you have an audience, a launch is a one-shot event. People form a view, tell each other, and mostly do not come back to check whether you improved. If you have spent years earning attention, spend the extra months making the first version genuinely good rather than merely viable.
sparks.why: The value of iterating in public depends on your audience size. Small audience means cheap mistakes and fast learning; large audience means a weak launch consumes goodwill you cannot rebuild at the same price.
sparks.apply: Before launching, ask honestly how many people are paying attention. Above a few thousand, raise your quality bar and delay rather than ship rough.

sparks.hook: Broadening your product is how focused competitors overtake you.
sparks.insight: Moz was excellent at one thing and then spent years and a great deal of money trying to become a full marketing platform, competing on every front at once against companies that each did only one of those fronts. The rebuild swallowed the roadmap, the original product stagnated, and the new one was never best at anything. Expansion feels like ambition and often it is a way of avoiding the harder work of being clearly better at the thing you already own.
sparks.why: Breadth splits engineering, support and marketing across fronts while a focused rival concentrates all of theirs on one. You lose on every axis simultaneously without ever making a single obviously bad decision.
sparks.apply: List your product areas and rank them by how close each is to being the best available. Cut or freeze everything outside your top one.

sparks.hook: Founding a company does not qualify you to run it.
sparks.insight: The person who can find a market and build the first version is not automatically the person who should manage two hundred employees, chair a board and run an operating plan. Those are different jobs requiring different skills, and enjoying the first one says little about the second. Fishkin eventually stepped out of the chief executive role and writes plainly about how long he stayed past the point where he knew. Self-awareness about which job you are good at is worth more than the resolve to endure the wrong one.
sparks.why: Founder and chief executive are conflated by convention and by ego, not by evidence. The skills correlate weakly, and the cost of the mismatch is paid by everyone in the company.
sparks.apply: Write out the parts of your role you dread, and ask whether they are temporary discomfort or a permanent mismatch with what you are good at.

sparks.hook: Your health is a company asset and you are depreciating it fast.
sparks.insight: Fishkin describes a stretch of severe depression while running the company, and is direct that the culture around him treated exhaustion as evidence of commitment. The arithmetic is simple and mostly ignored: a founder who cannot think clearly makes worse decisions, and in a small company decisions are the entire output. Sleep, treatment and time away are not rewards for hitting a target. They are inputs to the only asset the business genuinely cannot replace at short notice.
sparks.why: Sleep loss measurably degrades judgement and risk assessment. In a company where a handful of people make every consequential call, that degradation is a direct operating cost rather than a personal matter.
sparks.apply: Book the medical or therapeutic appointment you have deferred, this week, and put a recurring non-negotiable stop time in your calendar.

sparks.hook: A funding announcement is marketing, not a scoreboard.
sparks.insight: A rival raising a large round tells you that some investors made a bet, and nothing about whether the business works. The number is chosen partly for the press, the valuation reflects terms nobody publishes, and the announcement is timed for recruiting and sales rather than accuracy. Founders read these as evidence they are losing and reshape strategy in response. The only comparisons worth acting on are the ones you can verify: retention, revenue, and whether customers switch.
sparks.why: Announcements are a controlled disclosure by a party with an interest in appearing strong. Treating them as information about business quality is reading a company's own advertising as an audit.
sparks.apply: The next time a competitor announces a round, write down what it actually tells you about their customers. Then get back to your own retention numbers.

actions: Model your own equity at three exit prices, including a mediocre one, using the actual preference terms in your signed documents rather than the headline valuation.
Write down the outcome that would genuinely make you happy in seven years, then check whether your current funding structure can accommodate it.
Choose one number you have kept vague with your team and publish it internally along with your plan for it.
Book the health appointment you have been deferring and set a recurring weekly stop time that you defend as firmly as a customer meeting.
not_for_you_if: You want a tactical playbook with frameworks and checklists. This is a personal account whose value is in its honesty, not in a reusable system.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Fishkin co-founded Moz and later SparkToro. Prose here is original; no wording reproduced.

title: Super Founders
subtitle: What Data Reveals About Billion-Dollar Startups
author: Ali Tamaseb
why_it_matters: Someone finally went and gathered the data instead of retelling the folklore. Tamaseb compared hundreds of billion-dollar companies against a randomly drawn comparison group, and most of what the industry believes about founders did not survive.

crux.headline: Almost everything you believe about founders is folklore
crux.body: The picture of the young technical dropout, first to market with a novel idea and a co-founder from college, is drawn from a handful of famous cases. Compared against a control group, most of those traits fail to separate the companies that reached enormous scale from the ones that did not. What did stand out was prior experience of building something significant, and entering a market big enough to matter. Use the finding to stop disqualifying yourself.

sparks.hook: Compare winners against a control group and the folklore collapses.
sparks.insight: Almost all startup wisdom is drawn from famous companies only, which cannot tell you anything. If ninety percent of enormous successes had a particular trait, but ninety percent of failures had it too, the trait is worthless as a signal. Tamaseb built a dataset of billion-dollar companies alongside a randomly selected comparison group of startups that raised money and did not get there, then checked which characteristics actually differed. Most of the celebrated ones did not.
sparks.why: This is the base-rate problem in plain form. Any claim about what winners have in common is empty until somebody checks whether the losers have it in common too.
sparks.apply: Next time you hear a rule about what successful founders do, ask what proportion of failed founders also did it. If nobody checked, discount the rule.

sparks.hook: The billion-dollar founder is usually not in their twenties.
sparks.insight: The dropout-in-a-dorm image is drawn from a handful of unusually famous cases, and it does not describe the distribution. Founders of companies that reached extreme scale skew considerably older than the myth, with a great many starting in their thirties and forties, and older founders are not rarer among the biggest outcomes. Age brings the things that actually help: knowing an industry, knowing which problems are real, and having people who will take your call.
sparks.why: Independent work on entrepreneurial age using tax and census records has pointed the same way, finding that older founders are at least as likely to build fast-growing companies. Two different methods agreeing is worth something.
sparks.apply: If you have been treating your age as a reason not to start, replace that with an inventory of the industry knowledge and contacts you already hold.

sparks.hook: The strongest signal is having built something significant before.
sparks.insight: Across the comparisons, one attribute stood out more than the usual candidates: founders who had previously built something of real consequence, whether a company that reached meaningful scale, a widely used product, or an outstanding record inside a serious organisation. Not merely having founded something before, and certainly not having attended the right school. The pattern points to demonstrated capacity to make a difficult thing exist, which is far rarer than either credentials or enthusiasm.
sparks.why: A track record is an observed sample of your actual output rather than a proxy for it. Note that this is a correlation in one hand-built dataset, and prior success also buys access to capital and talent that others cannot get.
sparks.apply: If you have not built anything at scale yet, pick a project small enough to finish this year and large enough that finishing it proves something.

sparks.hook: You do not need a co-founder, and you do not need to be technical.
sparks.insight: Two rules of thumb are handed out constantly: find a co-founder, and make sure someone on the founding team can build the product. Neither separated the huge outcomes from the rest. Solo founders are well represented among companies that reached enormous scale, and so are teams where nobody wrote code. What matters is whether the specific business needs deep technical work, and whether you can attract people who supply what you lack. The general rule is not a rule.
sparks.why: The advice is really about coverage of critical skills, which many teams achieve by hiring rather than by co-founding. Turning it into a screening rule mostly filters on convention.
sparks.apply: List the three capabilities your business genuinely requires in its first year, then decide whether each is best covered by a founder, a hire or a contract.

sparks.hook: Competitors in your market are a good sign, not a warning.
sparks.insight: Founders panic when they find rivals and take comfort in an empty field. The data suggests the opposite reading. Companies that reached extreme scale frequently entered markets that already had competitors, sometimes many, and often arrived years after the first entrants. An empty market usually means no demand has been proven, whereas a crowded one means customers exist and are already paying somebody. The question is not whether rivals exist but whether the incumbents are actually good.
sparks.why: Competition is evidence of a market. The genuine risk is not rivalry but choosing a problem nobody is willing to pay to solve, which is invisible precisely because there is nobody to look at.
sparks.apply: Map the three closest competitors and interview five of their customers about what still annoys them. Treat a crowded field as validation to exploit.

sparks.hook: First-mover advantage is mostly a story told afterwards.
sparks.insight: Being early is celebrated because the winners of any market look, in retrospect, as if they had a head start. Many companies that reached the largest outcomes were not first at all. They arrived once the market had been proven by somebody else, learned from that company's mistakes, and executed better. Being first means paying for customer education and building on immature technology. Being second or fifth means somebody else absorbed those costs on your behalf.
sparks.why: Order of entry predicts far less than execution quality and timing of the underlying technology. Pioneers frequently spend their capital proving a market that a later entrant then wins.
sparks.apply: Stop treating a competitor's launch as a lost race. Write down the three things they are doing badly and make one of those your entire pitch.

sparks.hook: Four credentials the industry worships and the data barely notices.
sparks.insight: A cluster of things founders chase turn out to be weak separators between the enormous outcomes and everyone else. Elite university names, accelerator participation, patents held, and having a novel idea nobody has had before all appear on both sides of the comparison. They are not useless, and some open doors that matter. But treating them as prerequisites means declining to start until you have collected tokens that do not predict the thing you want.
sparks.why: These attributes are highly visible, which is why they get overweighted. Visibility and predictive power are different properties, and the first is what shapes how a community talks.
sparks.apply: Write down what you are waiting to acquire before starting. For each item, ask what evidence exists that it predicts anything, then start anyway.

carousel.title: Pedigree is weakly predictive
carousel.body: Elite degrees show up among huge successes and among ordinary startups alike. They help with access to investors, which is not the same as helping the company work.

carousel.title: Accelerators are not a filter
carousel.body: Programmes give structure, contacts and a deadline, all genuinely useful. Getting in is not evidence about the outcome, and being rejected is not evidence either.

carousel.title: Patents rarely decide it
carousel.body: Outside a few sectors such as pharmaceuticals, patents seldom separate the enormous outcomes from the rest. Distribution and execution usually decide who wins.

carousel.title: Novelty is overrated
carousel.body: Plenty of the largest companies did something already being done. Many also changed their idea substantially, so the original concept was not the asset anyway.

sparks.hook: The idea is negotiable. The size of the market is not.
sparks.insight: A great many companies that reached the largest outcomes ended up selling something meaningfully different from what they started with, which tells you the initial idea was rarely the decisive asset. What is much harder to change is the market you chose to enter. A brilliant execution inside a small market produces a small company, and a mediocre execution inside an enormous one can still produce a large one. Choose the pond deliberately, because you will keep changing the fish.
sparks.why: Product direction is cheap to alter and market position is not, since it determines your customers, your channels and your ceiling. Pivots within a market are common; pivots between markets usually mean starting again.
sparks.apply: Before your next big product decision, estimate how many customers exist in your chosen market and what they currently spend on this problem.

carousel.title: Count the actual buyers
carousel.body: Estimate how many organisations or people could realistically purchase, not the size of the industry a research firm describes in a headline.

carousel.title: Check what they spend today
carousel.body: Money already leaving their account for this problem is the clearest proof that a budget exists. A market with no current spending has to be created first.

carousel.title: Check the direction
carousel.body: A market shrinking slowly can look comfortable for years and then remove your whole business. Growth covers a great many execution mistakes; decline hides none.

carousel.title: Check you can reach them
carousel.body: Ask how you would contact a thousand of these buyers next month. A market you cannot address cheaply is somebody else's opportunity, not yours.

sparks.hook: This is a correlation study on a hand-built dataset. Read it that way.
sparks.insight: The comparison is far more rigorous than the anecdotes it replaces, and it is still not causal evidence. The company list was assembled by one investor, the control group required judgement calls to construct, the attributes were coded by hand, and none of it went through peer review. It also only covers companies that raised venture money, which excludes most businesses in the world. Treat the findings as a strong corrective to folklore rather than as a formula for predicting anything.
sparks.why: Descriptive comparison can rule things out convincingly while proving very little about what causes success. Rarity plus a small number of extreme outcomes makes statistical inference genuinely hard here.
sparks.apply: Use these findings to remove reasons you are not starting, and refuse to use them to predict whether a specific company will work.

sparks.hook: Use the data to disqualify fewer people, starting with yourself.
sparks.insight: The practical value of all this is negative rather than positive. It does not tell you who will build an enormous company, because nothing does. It does dismantle the reasons people give for not trying and the reasons investors give for passing: wrong age, no co-founder, not technical, not first, no famous degree. Each of those filters removes real candidates on evidence that does not hold up, which is expensive for the person filtered out and for whoever is doing the filtering.
sparks.why: Screening criteria with no predictive power still shape who gets funded, because they are easy to apply and they feel like judgement. That is how a whole industry can be systematically wrong for a long time.
sparks.apply: Write down every reason you think you are not the right person to start this. Cross out the ones this data contradicts, and address whatever is left.

actions: List the reasons you have given yourself for not starting, then mark each as either contradicted by the evidence here or a real gap you can close this year.
Estimate the size of your chosen market in customers and current spending, and treat that number as the ceiling on everything else you do.
Interview five customers of your nearest competitor about what still frustrates them, and turn the sharpest complaint into your positioning.
Identify one capability your first year genuinely requires, and decide explicitly whether to co-found, hire or contract for it.
not_for_you_if: You are building a small or bootstrapped business. The entire dataset is drawn from venture-funded companies chasing extreme outcomes, and little of it transfers.

verification.notes: Published 2021 by PublicAffairs. Tamaseb is a venture investor; the dataset is self-assembled and not peer reviewed, which the book itself acknowledges. Prose original.

title: The Cold Start Problem
subtitle: How to Start and Scale Network Effects
author: Andrew Chen
why_it_matters: Network effects were treated as a mystical property that either appeared or did not. This breaks them into a lifecycle with named stages and specific tactics, drawing on how marketplaces and social products were actually launched.

crux.headline: Do not launch a network. Launch one tiny network that works
crux.body: A product whose value comes from other users is worthless on day one, and no amount of marketing fixes an empty room. The escape is to ignore the market entirely and build the smallest group that is genuinely useful to itself: one campus, one office, one neighbourhood on one night. Get that group self-sustaining, then repeat it. Networks grow by copying a working cell, not by broadcasting to everyone at once.

sparks.hook: A network product is worthless on the day you launch it.
sparks.insight: Anything whose value comes from other people using it starts at zero and stays there until enough of them arrive. The first user of a messaging app has nobody to message. The first driver has no riders. This is not a marketing problem and cannot be spent past, because paid users arrive into an empty room and leave. Every successful network product got past this somehow, usually with tactics that look ridiculous at scale, and copying the mature version of a network tells you nothing about how it began.
sparks.why: Value depends on participation, so the product genuinely is bad early. Ordinary growth tactics assume the product already delivers value on arrival, which is precisely what is missing here.
sparks.apply: Write down what a single new user experiences if nobody else joins that week. If the answer is nothing, your first job is density rather than reach.

sparks.hook: Find the smallest group that would be useful to itself.
sparks.insight: The unit that matters is not the market, it is the smallest collection of people that keeps working without any help from you. For a workplace tool that might be one team of five in one office. For a ride service it might be a handful of drivers covering a few square miles on a Friday night. Get one of those to stability and you have proof plus a template.
